source: Zhang et al. (2026, ICLR) Darwin Godel Machine: open-ended evolution of self-improving agents
finding: Gap 1 and 3. The only LLM-agent study found that ablates the parent-allocation rule. Letting every archived agent be a parent beat always branching from the best agent, and beat keeping no archive.
numbers: Table 1 (80 iterations, one new agent per iteration; SWE-bench / Polyglot): DGM 50.0% / 38.0%; DGM Greedy (always best parent) 39.7% / 30.0%; DGM w/o open-ended exploration (no archive, latest agent only) 23.0% / 14.0%; DGM w/o self-improve 39.0% / 28.0%. Start was 20.0% on SWE-bench.
quote: allowing all solutions in the archive to serve as potential stepping stones can lead to greater improvements over time
limits: Same iteration count, not same tokens, and a single run per arm as far as the text shows. Agents are whole coding agents, not research directions. The no-archive arm is also harmed by broken self-edits.
agent_relevance: A rule that gives every untried or weak branch a non-zero chance beat pure follow-the-best by 10.3 points (SWE-bench) and 8.0 (Polyglot). Supports a code-set rule that keeps untried directions alive.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Darwin Godel Machine, Appendix C.2 parent selection
finding: Gap 3. The DGM parent weight is a soft cap: sigmoid of the agent's score divided by (1 + number of its children). More children means less chance to be picked.
numbers: Weight = sigmoid-scaled performance / (1 + n_children); sigmoid sharpness lambda = 10 (as printed). Only agents with working code-editing are eligible.
limits: No sweep of the crowding term itself. Only the whole rule was ablated (d01).
agent_relevance: A graded crowding penalty is an alternative to a hard cap of 2 per direction. Easy to code: weight = score_rank / (1 + attempts_in_direction). Untested against the hard cap.

source: Toledo et al. (2025) AI Research Agents for Machine Learning: Search, Exploration, and Generalization in MLE-bench (AIRA-dojo)
finding: Gap 2 and 3. With the weak operator set of AIDE, changing the search policy or the exploration constant did nothing. Exploration only paid once the operators (prompt design) were better.
numbers: MLE-bench Lite medal rate, 20 seeds, 24 h, R1: with AIDE operators, MCTS at UCT constant 0, 0.25, 0.75 and EVO all stayed near greedy (35.0 to 39.8 read from figure). With the new operators: AIRA greedy 45.5 vs AIDE greedy 39.8 (14% relative); AIRA MCTS 47.0 (best); all AIRA policies beat AIDE greedy.
quote: search policies yield no performance gain with AIDE's operators
limits: UCT sweep values are read from a figure. Reasoning models R1 and o3 only. Compute is wall-clock 24 h, not matched tokens. The authors say 3 seeds can reverse rankings; they recommend 10 to 20.
agent_relevance: No evidence that a more careful explore setting (like the UCT constant) matters on its own. The prompt that creates the attempt matters more. A threshold sweep (gap 2) is probably flat unless the attempt-generating prompt forces real novelty.

source: Toledo et al. (2025) AIRA-dojo: memory ablation and scoped memory
finding: Gap 8. For a single search agent that sees its own earlier attempts, a running memory of all previous designs and scores did not change medal rate. The authors then scoped memory to siblings to cut mode collapse.
numbers: AIDE with vs without the Memory operator: nearly identical mean medal rate (Fig. 3, 20 seeds). In AIRA operators: draft and improve see only sibling memories; debug sees the full ancestor chain; the AIRA operator set generates about 2x the completion tokens of AIDE's.
quote: memory is not a driving factor behind AIDE's strong performance
limits: Memory ablation only on the AIDE operator set. No test of the scoped-memory change alone, so its benefit is a design claim, not a measured effect.
agent_relevance: Shared notes across a single agent's own attempts are not a proven gain. If notes are kept, show only sibling attempts (what was already tried in this direction), not the leader board. Matches the follow-the-leader worry from Coral Discovery.

source: Toledo et al. (2025) AIRA-dojo: validation versus test score
finding: Gap 7 and G8. The agent's own validation score keeps rising while the held-out test score plateaus or falls. Picking the final answer by the agent's score loses a lot. Submitting a few top candidates recovers part of it.
numbers: Fig. 4a: perceived (validation) medal rate keeps improving over 24 h; true test rate plateaus, even slightly decreases (20 seeds). Selecting the best node in the final graph closes more than 60% of the gap to the oracle even for greedy agents. Top-3 submissions add about 10% performance; larger top-k vs random-k gap for MCTS and EVO suggests more diverse search graphs.
limits: Proxy fitness is 5-fold CV on the agent's own data, not an LLM self-rating. Still the closest measured case of a noisy internal score steering allocation.
agent_relevance: Allocation should not lean on the agent's own score alone. Use a code-computed score where one exists, and keep several candidates to the end.

source: Lange et al. (2025) ShinkaEvolve: towards open-ended and sample-efficient program evolution
finding: Gap 1, 3 and 4. Ablations on circle packing: weighted parent sampling beat random and pure hill-climbing; hill-climbing starts fast and plateaus; embedding novelty rejection beat no rejection.
numbers: Fig. 9 (about 150 evaluations, score axis 2.0 to 2.7). Weighted parent sampling (fitness and number of offspring) above hill climbing and best-of-N. Novelty filter: reject proposals with embedding similarity above 0.95; extra LLM novelty judge gave only marginal gain. Bandit LLM ensemble above fixed ensemble above single model.
quote: Hill climbing shows strong initial performance but plateaus quickly, while weighted sampling maintains steady improvement
limits: Results are curves in figures, no table and no error bars in the text; one task for the figure. 'Substantial' is the authors' word.
agent_relevance: Hill-climbing shows the same shape as the 76% champion concentration: fast early, stalls later. A 0.95 embedding filter is a cheap, code-set way to stop repeated directions (extends K16).

source: Zhang et al. (2026, ICML) Verbalized Sampling: how to mitigate mode collapse and unlock LLM diversity
finding: Gap 6. Asking the model for a list of answers with probabilities restores much of the lost diversity, and the user can tune it by asking for answers below a probability threshold. Gains are larger for bigger models.
numbers: Creative writing diversity 1.6 to 2.1x direct prompting. Human rating of diversity (1 to 4): poem 1.90 direct, 2.07 sequence, 2.39 VS; story 2.74, 2.76, 3.06; joke 1.83, 2.93, 3.01. Larger models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro) gain 1.5 to 2x more diversity than small ones (4.1-mini, 2.5-Flash).
limits: Tested on poems, stories, jokes, dialogue and synthetic data, not on research directions. Costs more tokens per call; small models can lose quality. The paper controls the total compute budget.
agent_relevance: A list-with-probabilities prompt for the direction proposal step is a cheap test. It still needs a code check for duplicates, because diversity of wording is not diversity of approach.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Verbalized Sampling, Table 3 synthetic data for math
finding: Gap 6. First measured link from prompt diversity to a final score: more diverse generated training questions gave higher downstream accuracy.
numbers: Average accuracy on MATH500, OlympiadBench, Minerva after fine-tuning on 1K synthetic questions (6 generator-student pairs): no-finetune baseline 32.8; Direct 30.6; Sequence 33.7; Multi-turn 34.3; VS-Standard 36.1; VS-CoT 37.5. Direct prompting data was worse than the baseline.
limits: Downstream score is of a student model, not of the generator's own search. Diversity of questions, not of solution approaches. No seeds reported in the table.
agent_relevance: Weak but real evidence that diversity at the proposal step can raise final score and not only novelty. Not yet shown for an agent choosing directions.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: is mixing different LLMs beneficial?
finding: Gap 6. Mixing different models gave worse results than sampling many times from the single best model. Diversity bought by weaker members costs quality.
numbers: Self-MoA beats Mixed-MoA by 6.6 points on AlpacaEval 2.0 and by 3.8 points on average over MMLU, CRUX and MATH. Self-MoA on the two best models gains 2 to 3 more points. Sequential Self-MoA is as good as one-shot aggregation.
limits: Aggregation of final answers, not direction search. Mixed-model gain exists when the models are specialised and similar in quality (they report such cases).
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to K12. Diversity from weaker or off-task proposers is not free. For one agent that has one model, vary the prompt, not the model quality.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents, Table 4 regression
finding: Gap 6. A direct test of whether diversity predicts score: both diversity and quality predict MoA performance, but quality has the larger weight on all three datasets in the standardised fit.
numbers: Fit t = alpha*q + beta*d on about 70 proposer mixtures per dataset (models plus 5 temperatures), z-scored. alpha (quality) / beta (diversity): MMLU 2.558 / 1.841, R2 0.771; CRUX 4.548 / 1.421, R2 0.685; MATH 4.719 / 2.839, R2 0.760; all p < 0.001. Diversity measured by Vendi score.
limits: Observational across mixtures, not randomised. Quality and diversity trade off on the Pareto front, so the two are correlated by design.
agent_relevance: Answers 'does diversity predict score, or only novelty': it does predict score, at about 0.3 to 0.7 the weight of quality here. Pick directions that are different AND not clearly weak.

source: Smit et al. (2024, ICML) Should we be going MAD? Multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Gap 10. Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat single-agent prompting plus self-consistency. It is more sensitive to settings. Tuned, one protocol surpasses the others.
numbers: Table 2 best accuracy: MedQA Medprompt 0.65, Society of Mind 0.64, Self-Consistency 0.60, Single Agent 0.60, Multi-Persona 0.58. MMLU Self-Consistency 0.78 vs Single Agent 0.76 vs Society of Mind 0.73. GPQA Single Agent 0.33 vs Society of Mind 0.27. Held-out hyperparameters: on non-medical sets single-agent methods beat all debate systems except one; on medical sets all but Multi-Persona beat single agent.
limits: Multiple-choice QA, not open-ended search. Accuracy differences of 1 to 3 points on small sets. Cost and time also reported in the paper.
agent_relevance: Coordination of simulated roles has a cost and gives no guaranteed gain. Do not add debate-style roles for division of labour; allocate by code instead (supports G9).

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Gap 10. Splits the failure rate by cause. Only one category is message passing between agents. Spec breaking and weak verification are the rest.
numbers: 1600+ annotated traces, 7 frameworks, failure rates 41% to 86.7% (ChatDev 86.7% on ProgramDev). Failure share: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%. Top modes: disobey task spec 44.2%, disobey role spec 32.3% (as printed in the mode table). Adding a task-objective verification step to ChatDev gave +15.6% task success on ProgramDev.
limits: No single-agent baseline in the study, so the overhead relative to one agent is not measured. Failure is judged by LLM annotators checked against human labels.
agent_relevance: A one-agent sequential scaffold has no inter-agent channel, so up to 36.9% of the failure mass (misalignment) cannot occur. The design (41.8%) and verification (21.3%) shares still apply. The code allocator needs a spec check and a verify step.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, The Social Dimensions of Scientific Knowledge (review)
finding: Gap 5. Review text gives the standing of the key results: Strevens ties division of labour to the priority rule; Muldoon and Weisberg reject Kitcher and Strevens as assuming ideal agents; Rosenstock et al. show the Zollman effect is parameter-sensitive.
numbers: No numbers of its own. States that adding nodes or widening the gap between the two hypotheses' probabilities drives the chance of consensus on the wrong hypothesis in dense networks to near zero.
quote: Adjust the number of nodes or the probabilities assigned to the alternative strategies/hypotheses and the Zollman effect disappears.
limits: Secondary source. Used only to date and frame the criticisms; the primary numbers for Rosenstock (2017) are not in our evidence.
agent_relevance: The 'less connection is better' result has a known robustness hole. Do not build a rule from it. Keep the allocation in code and do not hide results from the agent as a general policy.

source: Alexander, Himmelreich and Thompson (2015) Epistemic landscapes, optimal search, and the division of cognitive labor, Philosophy of Science 82
finding: Gap 5, abstract only (Crossref). Argues that a novelty-seeking strategy need not be optimal, that Weisberg and Muldoon showed no epistemic reason for division of labour, and names errors in their model. Also says to be sceptical of social learning in complex landscapes.
numbers: No numbers read. Full text paywalled; not opened.
quote: they have not shown epistemic reasons exist for the division of cognitive labor
limits: Abstract only. Cannot be cited for numbers.
agent_relevance: K03 (mavericks dominate) is contested by two independent papers (this and Thoma, d16). Treat the maverick result as model-dependent.

source: Rosenstock, Bruner and O'Connor (2017) In epistemic networks, is less really more? Philosophy of Science 84
finding: Gap 5, abstract only (Crossref). The Zollman and Kummerfeld results that sparse networks do better are not robust to parameter changes.
numbers: Abstract only. The SEP review (d13) reports the direction: more nodes or a bigger probability gap make the dense-network failure vanish.
quote: not robust across changes in parameter values
limits: Full text not opened; no simulation numbers.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication-by-extension for Zollman. Blocks any rule that says 'hide other attempts' for a single agent.

source: Thoma (2015) The epistemic division of labor revisited, Philosophy of Science 82
finding: Gap 5, abstract only (Crossref). Says Weisberg and Muldoon's result that all should be mavericks comes from implausible modelling choices; a changed model gives a gain from division of labour with one restriction.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers read here. Earlier records (K03/K04) already hold Thoma's numbers from another source.
quote: I argue that this is due to implausible modeling choices
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Pairs with d14: a mix of explorers and extractors beats pure mavericks once the model is fixed. Fits an explore-then-exploit split.

source: Grim, Singer, Bramson et al. (2019) Diversity, ability, and expertise in epistemic communities, Philosophy of Science 86
finding: Gap 5, abstract only (Crossref). Extends Hong and Page's model to landscapes of different randomness. The diversity-trumps-ability result is sensitive to the landscape. Authors advise against reading it broadly.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers read.
quote: we advise against interpreting such results overly broadly
limits: Full text not opened. The AMS Notices critique by Thompson (2014) returned HTTP 403 and was not read.
agent_relevance: K05 (Hong-Page, single-source) now has a second source saying it is landscape-sensitive. Downgrade to contested. Do not use diversity-beats-ability as a design basis.

source: Wu and O'Connor (2023) How should we promote transient diversity in science? Synthese
finding: Gap 9, abstract only (Crossref). Compares mechanisms from network models for keeping diversity of practice for a while, under ethical and practical limits. No field counts.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: No empirical count of researchers per approach. Still a modelling paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 not closed by this paper.

source: Smaldino, Moser, Perez Velilla and Werling (2024) Maintaining transient diversity is a general principle for improving collective problem solving, Perspectives on Psychological Science 19
finding: Gap 4. Reviews bandit, NK, cumulative-innovation and evolution models. Any mechanism that keeps solutions diverse longer raises final quality, at the cost of more time to reach it. Exceptions are easy problems and misaligned incentives.
numbers: Review, no single effect size. Lists mechanisms: sparse networks, slow interaction, noise in copying, behavioural inertia, wider search space.
limits: Review; individual studies are cited but their numbers are not in the extracted text. Human evidence in the review is mixed (shared-information bias in a caucus task).
agent_relevance: General support for explore-early, converge-later, and for the price: time. Does not give a schedule for how fast the explore share should fall.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster and Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery, PNAS 112
finding: Gap 9. A field-data study: 30 years of MEDLINE papers and patents. Real scientists choose conservative problems around well-studied molecules, and this becomes more conservative over time. The model says that is inefficient for science as a whole.
numbers: The inferred MEDLINE strategy peaks in efficiency at 13% of the network discovered; to discover the bulk of the network it is over 3 times more costly than the best alternative strategy; the best strategy for 50% discovery is nearly 10 times more efficient than random uncoordinated choice. Publishing failures speeds discovery.
limits: Model-based inference on a biomedical chemistry network, not counts of researchers per named approach. No peptic-ulcer case counts. Ratios come from simulation on a sample of the graph.
agent_relevance: Real researchers fail to spread; the human crowd drifts to the safe direction. Same pattern as agents following the leader. It is not a direct count for gap 9, so gap 9 stays partly open.

source: Own simulation (2026-11-01): Kitcher-style allocation with noisy success estimates
finding: Gap 7. Credit-seeking allocation (each researcher joins the project with the best personal expected credit) loses its advantage when the success estimates are noisy. With log-noise sd 0.25 to 0.5 it falls below a plain equal split; at chance-level estimates it is far below it.
numbers: 5 projects, 50 researchers, return = sum q_i*(1-exp(-a n_i)), 4000 trials, % of true optimum. a=0.02 (slow saturation), noise sd 0/0.25/0.5/1/2/chance: credit 98.1/90.5/81.9/72.7/66.0/70.4; equal split 83.4 to 83.6 (flat); all-in on perceived best 84.5/79.4/73.8/68.2/63.5/57.4; planner optimum on noisy estimates 100/95.3/87.3/76.8/68.6/75.4. a=0.05: credit 96.9/90.6/79.8/66.0/55.4/74.9; equal split 91.2; all-in 62.0/58.2/54.4/49.8/46.6/42.7.
limits: Own toy model written for this gap, not from the literature. Results depend on the return curve and the noise form (multiplicative log-normal). Not peer reviewed. 'Chance' means estimates drawn independent of truth.
agent_relevance: Supports putting the quota in code: a fixed spread ignores the self-ratings and holds 83 to 91% of optimum at any noise, while rating-driven allocation drops under it once estimates are about +-30 to +-65% off. All-in on the self-rated best is worst throughout.

source: Own simulation (2026-11-01): one agent, 30 sequential attempts over 10 directions, free versus code-set allocation
finding: Gaps 1 and 3. At equal attempt count, a code-set spread beats free self-chosen directions when the agent's own prior about which direction is best is weak, and loses when the prior is strong. A cap of 2 per direction followed by exploit was the best code rule tested.
numbers: 10 directions with ceilings ~N(0,1); direction value = ceiling*(1-exp(-n/3)); observed score has noise sd 0.5; 3000 trials; score = true value of the attempt the agent submits (picked by observed score). Prior skill rho 0 / 0.3 / 0.6 (beta 1): free 0.695 / 0.884 / 1.066; quota (one per direction then exploit) 0.793 / 0.772 / 0.774; cap 2 then exploit 0.940 / 0.961 / 0.956; free then lock on to best-so-far 0.463 / 0.632 / 0.802. Cap 3 (explores to the end) 0.683 / 0.678 / 0.668; cap 1 about 0.77 to 0.81. SE about 0.01 to 0.015. With stronger mode collapse (beta 3) free falls to 0.525 at rho 0.
limits: Own toy model. Equal attempts treated as equal tokens. Learning-curve time constant (3) and noise were chosen by me. Crossover between code-set and free is near prior skill rho 0.3 to 0.6 here for quota, above 0.6 for cap 2; no real measure of an LLM's rho exists in our evidence (G8 says model judges rank near chance).
agent_relevance: Prediction to test: if the model's own direction ranking is weak, a code spread with cap 2 then a champion phase should beat free attempts by about 0.25 to 0.3 in score units (about a quarter of the spread of direction ceilings); if the ranking is good (rho >= 0.6) free attempts win. Test needed on a real task at equal tokens.

source: Own simulation (2026-11-01): pivot threshold and explore share sweeps, with sensitivity to learning speed
finding: Gaps 2 and 4. In the same toy, the best pivot threshold was 2 non-improving attempts when directions improve fast, and the result was flat when they improve slowly; 5 was never clearly best. The best explore share was about 70% of the budget, not early-only.
numbers: Pivot to a code-chosen untried direction after m non-improving attempts, tau = 3: m=1 0.862, m=2 0.923, m=3 0.859, m=5 0.809, m=8 0.674, m=12 0.523 (SE 0.012 to 0.015). tau = 1: m=2 1.293 best, m=5 0.995. tau = 6: m=1 0.582, m=2 0.540, m=3 0.519, m=5 0.593, m=8 0.547 (1500 trials, SE about 0.02, all within noise). Explore share (untried directions first, then best-so-far), tau 3: 0.2 gives 0.687, 0.33 0.780, 0.5 0.901, 0.7 0.986, 1.0 (never exploit) 0.666. tau 1: 0.7 best at 1.303; tau 6: 0.5 best 0.560.
limits: Own toy model, same caveats as d22. Optimal m and explore share depend on the unknown speed of improvement within a direction. Not a recommendation for a real run; a design for one.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable shape: threshold curve peaks at a low value and falls past about 5; explore share should reach exploit for roughly the last 30% of attempts rather than never. A real sweep on one open task at equal tokens is still needed.
